intro: Cellos and woodwinds begin a chain of phrases that approach a cadence without finding rest. These two excerpts use different performances: Simon Schindler’s Fulda orchestra here, Nanny Larsen-Todsen’s historical vocal recording in the Liebestod.
question: How can a chord resolve without bringing the phrase to rest?

cues.title: The chord in bar two
cues.text: The opening cello gesture leads to F–B–D♯–G♯ in bar 2: the Tristan chord. Its continuation reaches another unstable harmony, E7, rather than the expected A-minor resting place.
cues.evidence: https://www.laits.utexas.edu/tristan/prelude.php and https://www.laits.utexas.edu/tristan/motive1-3.php identify the written opening. The report places the first sounding phrase around 0:05–0:20; bar 2 is not aligned to an exact second.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Silence without a cadence
cues.text: Across the opening statements, the rests separate phrases without giving the ear a settled tonic. Keep the ascending semitone line in mind when each new attempt begins.
cues.evidence: Analysis: quiet windows at 0:20–0:25 and 0:45 separate stronger phrases. The repeated opening and chromatic line are shown in the University of Texas score analysis.

cues.title: Small intervals accumulate
cues.text: Wagner’s rising G♯–A–A♯–B line climbs by semitone. The pitches are close together, but each step changes its relation to the harmony underneath; melodic motion and harmonic arrival need not coincide.
cues.evidence: https://www.laits.utexas.edu/tristan/prelude.php shows the first seventeen bars. This is a general account of their construction, not a claim that all four pitches occur at 1:15.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Phrases start to connect
cues.text: After the separated opening attempts, the score lets the phrases overlap and gives the strings a larger melodic role. Listen for continuity replacing the opening’s repeated stops.
cues.evidence: Score pp. 3–4: https://hdl.handle.net/1802/13070. Analysis has a boundary at 1:34 and a marked level rise by 1:35; the entrance of the larger span is approximate.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Desire and philosophy
cues.text: Wagner encountered Schopenhauer’s philosophy in 1854, before composing Tristan. The opera turns desire into a musical process: apparent goals become beginnings rather than final answers.
cues.evidence: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tristan_und_Isolde; the University of Texas analysis relates the Prelude’s desire motif to Schopenhauer.

cues.title: Separate the musical layers
cues.text: Throughout the broader phrases, follow the bass separately from the upper melody. A line can keep climbing while the harmony underneath avoids the point of rest that its contour appears to promise.
cues.evidence: General listening suggestion based on the independent orchestral lines in the full score, pp. 4–6: https://hdl.handle.net/1802/13070
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A retreat within expansion
cues.text: This stretch withdraws before another rise. Do not treat the drop in intensity as the end of the argument: the music can reduce its weight without resolving the harmonic question.
cues.evidence: Analysis: relative level falls from −15.7 dB at 3:25 to −37.3 dB at 3:45, then rises to −19.2 dB by 4:05.

cues.title: Recognising a rhythm
cues.text: The figure often called the “glance” motif has a characteristic rhythm as well as its rising intervals. Compare rhythmic shapes when changing harmony makes a melody less immediately familiar.
cues.evidence: The University of Texas illustrates the glance rhythm and its derivation: https://www.laits.utexas.edu/tristan/prelude2.php. No individual statement is time-aligned.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A longer accumulation
cues.text: The central ascent sustains its pressure for longer than the opening’s brief attempts. Repeated melodic shapes move through changing harmonies; the enlargement comes from joining and intensifying familiar material.
cues.evidence: Analysis boundaries at 4:44 and 4:58 precede a sustained rise through 5:45–5:50. Score-informed passage description, not a bar-level alignment.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Rising without arriving
cues.text: In this part of the ascent, the recorded level increases before easing again. Listen through the smaller crest: Wagner places local releases inside a larger, unfinished span.
cues.evidence: Analysis rises from −19.4 dB at 5:30 to −13.5 dB at 5:50, then drops to −19.1 dB at 6:05.

cues.title: An interrupted Ring
cues.text: Wagner set Siegfried aside in 1857 after its second act. He completed Tristan in 1859 and did not resume Siegfried’s third act until 1869.
cues.evidence: Wagner work chronology: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Wagner; also the site’s Wagner biography.

cues.title: The scale of the crest
cues.text: Compare the extended late ascent with the short opening phrases. The orchestra keeps accumulating weight across a span that once would have been interrupted by silence.
cues.evidence: Analysis: high relative levels persist from 6:40 through 7:40; the loudest five-second window is 7:35.

cues.title: Pressure falls away
cues.text: After the largest crest, the recorded sound drops sharply. The return to quieter writing is not a repetition of the opening at its original size: the accumulated tension changes how the sparse phrases are heard.
cues.evidence: Analysis: −7.9 dB at 7:35, −23.2 at 7:45, −37.1 at 7:50; novelty boundary at 7:48. Score pp. 12–13 supplies the thinning texture.

cues.title: A concert ending
cues.text: This file is labelled “Konzertfassung”, a concert version. In the opera the Prelude gives way to the young sailor’s song; here the orchestra must provide an ending without the stage action.
cues.evidence: Commons embedded title explicitly says Konzertfassung. The performed concert-ending edition is unidentified; no precise splice or final bar number is asserted.

cues.title: Six years to the stage
cues.text: The completed opera waited until 10 June 1865 for its Munich première, conducted by Hans von Bülow. Ludwig II’s support made the production possible; the Prelude had already circulated in concert.
cues.evidence: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tristan_und_Isolde documents completion, première and earlier concert performances.

cues.title: Recall the first question
cues.text: Keep the opening’s unstable harmonies in memory while the concert conclusion unfolds. A self-contained ending answers a practical concert-hall need; it does not reproduce the opera’s passage into Act I.
cues.evidence: Commons identifies a concert version; this is a whole-version comparison, not a claim about an individual chord at 9:50.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The quieter conclusion
cues.text: The conclusion stays well below the earlier crest in recorded level. Follow the space between attacks and the sustained resonance rather than expecting another large orchestral climax.
cues.evidence: Analysis: 10:20–10:50 windows lie roughly −26 to −31 dB, compared with −7.9 dB at the main crest.

cues.title: Let the resonance finish
cues.text: The final sound gives way to silence within the last few seconds. Leave room for that decay after the long concert conclusion.
cues.evidence: Analysis: −34.8 dB at 10:55, −31.9 at 11:00, then −73.5 at 11:05. This locates the ending passage, not a final-note attack.

transitions.title: Rests give way to connected phrases
transitions.how: The opening’s cello and woodwind exchanges repeatedly approach dominant harmony and stop. The continuation brings the strings into a more connected phrase, retaining the semitone motion but replacing isolated attempts with overlapping lines. The join changes phrase continuity rather than supplying an unequivocal tonic cadence.
transitions.evidence: Score pp. 3–4; analysis boundary 1:34 and level rise by 1:35. Timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The same tension gains more weight
transitions.how: The orchestra expands the connected idea through repeated rising shapes and moving inner parts. The chromatic line survives the change of density: larger scoring and renewed harmonic motion extend the preceding phrase rather than introducing a self-contained song.
transitions.evidence: Analysis boundary 2:50, followed by the stronger 3:05 and 3:25 windows; score pp. 4–6.

transitions.title: Local swells become a sustained ascent
transitions.how: Wagner joins successive rises through chromatic voice-leading. String figuration moves beneath sustained wind lines, so the passing of one melodic crest does not stop the accompaniment. Sequences carry the argument onwards instead of closing it with a stable tonic.
transitions.evidence: Analysis boundaries 4:44 and 4:58; score pp. 6–10. No machine key estimate is treated as an individual chord.

transitions.title: The motives converge at the crest
transitions.how: The rising desire figure and the characteristic glance rhythm converge in the score’s late climax. Strings, winds and brass enlarge material that began in a small woodwind-and-cello exchange; the crescendo intensifies the same unresolved directional pressure.
transitions.evidence: University of Texas prelude part 4 identifies bars 74–83; the strongest recorded crest falls around 7:30–7:40. No bar onset is aligned.

transitions.title: The orchestra sheds its accumulated weight
transitions.how: The crest recedes through diminishing dynamics and thinner scoring. Short fragments again become exposed above a reduced accompaniment. The continuity established in the central span loosens, but withdrawal is not the same thing as a decisive tonal answer.
transitions.evidence: Analysis boundary 7:48 and the approximately thirty-decibel fall across 7:35–7:50; score pp. 12–13.

transitions.title: The excerpt makes its own conclusion
transitions.how: The concert version continues towards a self-contained orchestral close rather than the sailor’s unaccompanied stage song. The preceding low-level texture gives way to a more sustained concluding passage. The source does not name the concert-ending edition, so its individual chords and instrumental allocations are not assigned here.
transitions.evidence: Analysis boundary 8:40 precedes a sustained quieter final span. Commons calls the file Konzertfassung; the exact concert-ending score is unestablished.

facts: Composition with Theodor Weinlig in Leipzig; practical theatre work in Würzburg, Magdeburg, Königsberg and Riga
Royal Saxon Kapellmeister, Dresden, 1843–49; founder of the Bayreuth Festival, first held in 1876
Wrote his own librettos, alongside extensive and often polemical prose
Thirteen completed operas; the four-part Ring; songs, orchestral works and piano music
composer.background:
Wagner grew up among actors, singers and theatrical households in Leipzig and Dresden. His father died in 1813; his mother subsequently married the actor and painter Ludwig Geyer. Literature preceded serious musical training: as a schoolboy Wagner attempted a tragedy before he had mastered composition. Beethoven’s symphonies and Weber’s operas supplied different models, one for the weight of an orchestral argument, the other for a German theatre of supernatural events and sharply characterised instruments. Lessons with Theodor Weinlig in 1831 gave him a grounding in counterpoint. The later claim to have rebuilt opera came from someone who first learned its routines as a working theatre musician.

He held posts in Würzburg, Magdeburg, Königsberg and Riga, married the actress Minna Planer in 1836, and repeatedly found himself in debt. His early operas tried incompatible languages: Die Feen follows German Romantic opera, while Das Liebesverbot, after Shakespeare’s Measure for Measure, adopts a more Italianate manner. In 1839 the Wagners fled Riga and travelled by sea to London, then to Paris. There he copied, arranged and wrote journalism while trying to enter the operatic establishment. Meyerbeer, whom Wagner would later attack, helped him obtain a hearing for Rienzi. Wagner knew the grand-opera machinery of public ceremony, political catastrophe and large chorus from practical experience.
composer.epithet: An opera composer who made the orchestra remember what the characters conceal, and built a theatre for the result.
